papers.title_in_file: PHOTON-PAIR GENERATION IN A HETEROGENEOUS SILICON PHOTONIC CHIP
papers.version_note: arXiv:2208.13955v1, 30 Aug 2022. The text layer holds the paper once, 8 pages. Table 1 is flattened column by column, so its rows are read by column order.
papers.what_it_is: An experimental paper reporting photon-pair and heralded single-photon generation by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a hydrogenated amorphous silicon waveguide routed through low-loss silicon nitride waveguides on one chip.

assertions.value: The authors report a highest coincidence-to-accidental ratio (CAR) of 1632.6 (± 260.4) at an average on-chip pump power of about -30.5 dBm, with a corresponding photon pair generation rate of 1.94 MHz.
quotes: The highest CAR is achieved at 1632.6 (± 260.4) with average on-chip pump power of about -30.5 dBm.
The corresponding photon pair generation rate (PGR) is measured and estimated to be 1.94 MHz.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical result from one device and one run series.
assertions.reader_inference: The CAR is for dark-count-subtracted counts (see the dark-count assertion); the pair rate is derived from singles and coincidence rates (see the PGR definition), not counted directly.

assertions.value: The authors state that the CAR of 1632.6 (± 260.4) is a record high for non-resonant a-Si:H waveguides and a 4-times improvement over the previous single-layer a-Si:H platform.
quotes: we have experimentally demonstrated photon-pair generation with a record high CAR of 1632.6 (± 260.4) for non-resonant a-Si:H waveguides
which shows 4-times improvement compared to the previous single-layer a-Si:H platform
assertions.certainty_reason: A priority and comparison claim by the authors, against one earlier result (Wang et al. 2014) and a table of selected works.
assertions.reader_inference: The record is limited to non-resonant a-Si:H waveguides. Table 1 of the same paper lists higher CAR values for other platforms (see the Table 1 assertion). Table 1 gives 399 for the earlier a-Si:H result, a ratio of 4.09.

assertions.value: The authors state that, against the previous result in a pure a-Si:H platform, their device has 4 times higher CAR and 30 times higher PGR, and they attribute this to much lower propagation and coupling loss through the waveguide.
quotes: our device has exhibited 4 times higher CAR and 30 times higher PGR due to much lower
propagation/coupling loss through the waveguide.
assertions.certainty_reason: The attribution to lower loss is the authors' explanation; the paper does not test it by a control experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 1 gives 65 kHz for the earlier a-Si:H result and 1.94 MHz for this work, a ratio of about 30. The comparison mixes different pump powers, filters and detectors.

assertions.value: The authors report that the CAR drops to 1335.3 (± 240.9) when the on-chip pump power is lowered further, and they explain this by background noise contributing more when the Stokes and anti-Stokes count rates approach the dark-count level.
quotes: The CAR then drops to 1335.3 (± 240.9) when further lowering on-chip pump power.
the background noise contributes more to the result when the count rates of Stokes and anti-Stokes photons are closer to the dark-count level.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical observation with the authors' explanation; the explanation is not tested separately.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a stated limit of the CAR figure: the CAR peaks at an intermediate pump power and is not a monotone function of power.

assertions.value: The authors state that the dark count has been subtracted from the coincidence and accidental counts before the CAR is computed.
quotes: The dark count has been subtracted from coincidence and accidental counts to eliminate dark-count noise
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own data-processing step in Section 2, p.4.
assertions.reader_inference: The quoted CAR values are therefore not raw CAR values and are not directly comparable with works that do not subtract dark counts. The paper does not state whether the compared works in Table 1 did.

assertions.value: The authors define the photon pair generation rate as estimated by N1 times N2 divided by N12, where N1, N2 and N12 are the detection rates of signal, idler and two-photon coincidences.
quotes: The PGR is then estimated as N1N2/N12, where N1, N2 and N12 donates the detection rate of signal, idler and two-photon coincidences.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the estimator in Section 2, p.4.
assertions.reader_inference: The ratio N1N2/N12 uses detected rates only. It is a rate at the source if the signal and idler channels have equal transmission and detection efficiency, which the paper does not state.

assertions.value: The authors report that with an on-chip pump power of -20.5 dBm and a programmable waveshaper in place of the DWDM filters, the CAR remains about 200 for wavelength detuning from 4.2 nm to 10.2 nm, and that the waveshaper adds 5 dB loss which raises the required pump power.
quotes: With on-chip pump power at -20.5 dBm, the CAR remains about 200 for the wavelength detuning from 4.2 nm to 10.2 nm.
The waveshaper introduces an additional 5 dB loss, which increases the required pump power.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical measurement series on one device.
assertions.reader_inference: The 4.2 nm to 10.2 nm span is 6 nm wide.

assertions.value: The authors describe the multi-channel bandwidth differently in three places: the Introduction says a detuning bandwidth of 6 nm, the body text says detuning from 4.2 nm to 10.2 nm, and the Conclusion says a CAR of around 200 across a 10-nm bandwidth.
assertions.anchor: Introduction p.2; Section 2 p.4; Conclusion p.5
quotes: multiple channels with a detuning bandwidth of 6 nm and CAR value consistently at 200
the CAR remains about 200 for the wavelength detuning from 4.2 nm to 10.2 nm
multi-channel photon-pair sources with a CAR of around 200 across 10-nm bandwidth
assertions.certainty_reason: A reading of three statements in one paper; the measured range is in Figure 4(d), which the text layer does not carry.
assertions.reader_inference: The measured span (detuning 4.2 nm to 10.2 nm) is 6 nm wide and its upper end is 10.2 nm, so the Introduction and Conclusion use different readings of one result. The Section 2 statement is the most specific.

assertions.value: The authors report a lowest heralded auto-correlation gH(2)(0) of 0.0126 ± 0.005 at an on-chip power of -22.5 dBm and a signal rate N1 of 18 kHz, rising to 0.1085 ± 0.0014 at -16.3 dBm and N1 of 310 kHz.
quotes: The lowest gH(2)(0) is measured to be 0.0126 ± 0.005 at an on-chip power of -22.5 dBm and N1 of 18 kHz.
It increases to 0.1085 ± 0.0014 at on-chip power of -16.3 dBm and N1 of 310 kHz.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one device.
assertions.reader_inference: The auto-correlation rises with pump power, as expected when multi-pair emission grows. The uncertainty on the lowest value (0.005) is large relative to the value.

assertions.value: The abstract reports a lowest gH(2)(0) of 0.1085 ± 0.0014, whereas the main text gives 0.0126 ± 0.005 as the lowest value, 0.1085 ± 0.0014 as the value at higher power, and the Conclusion gives 0.0125 ± 0.005.
assertions.anchor: Abstract p.1; Section 2 p.4; Conclusion p.5
quotes: Lastly, we measure heralded single-photons with a lowest gH(2)(0) of 0.1085 ± 0.0014.
The lowest gH(2)(0) is measured to be 0.0126 ± 0.005
demonstrated low correlation function of gH(2)(0) at 0.0125 ± 0.005
assertions.certainty_reason: Three statements in one paper disagree; a reader cannot settle which figure is intended from the text alone.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract figure of 0.1085 contradicts the body, where it is the value at higher power. The conclusion's 0.0125 differs from the body's 0.0126 in the last digit. The body and Table 1 (0.0126) agree, so 0.0126 is the best-supported lowest value.

assertions.value: The authors state that gH(2)(τ) is calculated as N123 times N1 divided by N12 times N13, from double coincidences of the signal with idler I (N12) and idler II (N13) and triple coincidences N123, with the idler split by a 50/50 splitter and zero-delay values normalized to the average at other 20 ns delays.
quotes: the idler is separated by a 50/50 splitter into two as idler I and idler II
The auto-correlation function of gH(2)(τ ) is then calculated by N123N1/N12N13, where N1 donates signal detection rate.
which is normalized to the averaged gH(2)(τ ) at other 20 ns-delays (corresponding to the 50 MHz repetition rate of our MLL)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the estimator and normalization in Section 2, p.4.
assertions.reader_inference: The normalization to other pulse delays treats accidental coincidences between pulses as the baseline, so the quoted value is a ratio to that baseline.

assertions.value: The authors state that duplicating the detected photon channel into multiple virtual channels with different time delays lets all corresponding coincidences be measured at once, within the same experimental run, which they say largely simplifies the experiment and reduces noise and instabilities from different runs.
quotes: This is enabled by duplicating the detected physical photon channel to multiple virtual channels with different time delays
This method largely simpli
reduces noise and instabilities induced by different experimental runs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The benefit is an author statement without a comparison measurement.

assertions.value: The authors describe the fabrication: a 100-mm silicon wafer with 3-µm thermal oxide, 240 nm of SiNx by low-pressure chemical vapor deposition at 775 oC, then 225-nm of a-Si:H by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition at 300 oC, with the a-Si:H waveguides patterned by e-beam lithography and reactive ion etching.
quotes: The device fabrication starts with a 100-mm silicon wafer with a 3-µm thick layer of thermal oxide on its surface. 240 nm of SiNx is deposited using low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD).
a temperature of 775 oC
225-nm of a-Si:H was then deposited by PECVD.
a temperature of 300 oC
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own fabrication recipe in Section 2, p.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the lower a-Si:H deposition temperature lets them deposit it directly on top of the SiNx waveguides without damaging them.
quotes: With the lower a-Si:H deposition temperature we are able to deposit it directly on top of the SiNx waveguides without damaging them.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement of the reason for the process choice, without a damage test in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The introduction also cites lower deposition temperature as the reason a-Si:H fits mass chip manufacturing (see the cited Hemsley 2016 statement).

assertions.value: The authors report an on-chip interlayer coupling insertion loss below 1 dB per transition over a 100 nm bandwidth, propagation losses of 0.5 dB/cm in SiNx and 4 dB/cm in a-Si:H, and a total on-off chip loss of 9 dB.
quotes: The on-chip interlayer coupling insertion loss is measured to be less than 1 dB per transition over a 100 nm bandwidth
the propagation losses in the SiNx and a-Si:H waveguides are 0.5 dB/cm and 4 dB/cm, respectively
The total on-off chip loss is 9 dB.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured device figures from one fabrication run.
assertions.reader_inference: The introduction says the coupling loss is optimized around 0.5 dB per transition in the earlier design, while the measured bound here is less than 1 dB per transition.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing their previous work, that a careful design of the vertical coupler optimizes the coupling loss to around 0.5 dB per transition, and that using Si3N4 for on/off-chip coupling dramatically reduces fiber-to-fiber loss and the required pump power.
quotes: With a careful design of vertical coupler, the coupling loss is optimized around 0.5 dB per transition.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to MacFarlane et al. [2019], not measured in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors report a Kerr coefficient of about 5 x 10 to the power of minus 13 square centimeters per watt, equated from degenerate four-wave mixing conversion efficiency measured on devices with a-Si:H lengths between 1 mm and 5.5 mm, and call it comparable to the state-of-the-art value of 7.43 x 10 to the power of minus 13.
quotes: These results equate to a Kerr coefficient of ∼ 5 x 10−13 cm2/W, which is comparable to the state-of-the-art value (7.43 x 10−13 cm2/W)
propagates for varying a-Si:H lengths between 1 mm and 5.5 mm
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical estimate from conversion-efficiency fits; the fit is in Figure 2(b), which the text layer does not carry.
assertions.reader_inference: The measured value is about two thirds of the cited value; whether that is within error is not stated.

assertions.value: The authors cite Wang and Foster for a Kerr nonlinearity of n2 = 7.43 ± 0.87 x 10 to the power of minus 13 square centimeters per watt for a-Si:H, which they call ultra-high compared with other silicon-based platforms, and state that efficient SFWM can then be reached with only millimeters of waveguide propagation.
quotes: its ultra-high Kerr nonlinearity (n2 = 7.43 ± 0.87x10−13 cm2/W ) comparing to other silicon-based material platforms
efficient SFWM can be achieved with only millimeters of waveguide propagation
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors cite Oo et al. that the lowest reported a-Si:H linear propagation losses are about an order of magnitude higher than Si3N4, and state that this high loss leaves many photon pairs lost on chip before off-chip detection, which reduces the observable CAR.
quotes: the lowest reported a-Si:H linear propagation losses are about an order of magnitude higher than Si3N4
the high propagation loss of a-Si:H waveguide resuts in many of the photon pairs being lost on chip before off-chip detection.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work, with the authors' consequence stated as motivation.
assertions.reader_inference: This paper's own figures are 4 dB/cm for a-Si:H and 0.5 dB/cm for SiNx, a factor of 8.

assertions.value: The authors describe the pump as a 50 MHz mode-locked laser filtered by four cascaded DWDM filters at 1552.5 nm, coupled in the TE waveguide mode into a 2.5 mm long a-Si:H waveguide, with Stokes photons collected at 1545.3 nm and anti-Stokes photons at 1559.7 nm through 200 GHz DWDM filters.
quotes: a 50MHz mode lock laser(Calmar Mendocino)
four cascaded dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM)
at 1552.5 nm
a 2.5 mm long a-Si:H waveguide where the photon-pair is generated
at 1545.3 nm collect Stokes photons
The anti-Stokes photon at 1559.7nm is collected by two other DWDMs.
The bandwidth for the DWDM ﬁlters are aligned to be 200 GHz.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Section 2, p.3.
assertions.reader_inference: The bandwidth of 200 GHz is stated in the sentence 'The bandwidth for the DWDM filters are aligned to be 200 GHz.'; the 50 MHz repetition rate gives the 20 ns pulse spacing used in the g2 normalization.

assertions.value: The authors report detection with 4-channel superconducting nanowire single photon detectors (ID281, ID Quantique) with a dark-count rate of 50-100 Hz and a detection efficiency of 85%, read out by a time-tagging unit from Swabian Instruments, with output DWDM sets adding 1.9 dB loss at the Stokes channel and 2.2 dB at the anti-Stokes channel, and pump rejection by two cascaded DWDM filters of labelled 60 dB extinction.
quotes: The SNSPDs have dark-count rate of 50-100 Hz and detection efficiency of 85%.
The total losses by the output DWDM sets are 1.9 dB and 2.2 dB at Stokes and anti-Stokes channels, respectively.
two cascaded DWDM
with labelled 60 dB extinction
(4 channels SNSPDs, ID281, ID Quantique)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own detection setup in Section 2, pp.3-4.
assertions.reader_inference: The 60 dB figure is the filter's label, not a measurement by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors state that SRS-generated photons in the waveguide are linearly proportional to the on-chip pump power while SFWM-generated photons scale with the square of the pump power (printed flat as Pi2n in the text layer), and that the SRS noise is extracted at the Stokes and anti-Stokes channels by fitting the single-photon count curves.
quotes: the SRS generated photons are linearly proportional to the on-chip pump power Pin while the SFWM generated photons are proportional to Pi2n.
SRS noise can be abstracted at Stokes and anti-Stokes channels by
assertions.certainty_reason: A scaling statement used to separate noise from signal; the fit itself is in Figure 3(b), which the text layer does not carry.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no fitted SRS coefficient in text.

assertions.value: The authors' comparison table compares chi(3) photon-pair sources across nine rows, listing CAR values of 399, 1632.6, 373.3, 274, 2610, 12105, 532, 2280 and 4389, for materials from a-Si:H, a-Si:H/Si3N4, c-Si disk, c-Si ring, Si3N4 ring and AlGaAsOI ring.
quotes: a-Si:H a-Si:H/Si3N4 a-Si:H/Si3N4
c-Si disk c-Si disk c-Si ring c-Si ring Si3N4 ring AlGaAsOI ring
assertions.certainty_reason: A literature comparison table assembled by the authors; the text layer flattens it by column.
assertions.reader_inference: By column order the two 'This work' rows are CAR 1632.6 at 0.9 µW with PGR 1.94 MHz, and CAR 373.3 at 5.6 µW with PGR 3.29 MHz and gH(2) 0.0126. The table lists higher CAR for a c-Si ring (12105, Ma 2017), an AlGaAsOI ring (4389, Steiner 2021) and a c-Si disk (2610, Lu 2016), so the 1632.6 record holds only within non-resonant a-Si:H waveguides, as the paper states.

assertions.value: The authors' Table 1 lists on-chip pump powers of 18 µW, 0.9 µW, 5.6 µW, 79 µW, 12µW, 7.4 µW, 59 µW, 46 µW and 3.4 µW, and photon pair generation rates of 65 kHz, 1.94 MHz, 3.29 MHz, 855 kHz, 1.2 kHz, 16 kHz, 1.1 MHz, 4.8 kHz and 230KHz.
quotes: On-chip pump power 18 µW 0.9 µW 5.6 µW 79 µW 12µW 7.4 µW 59 µW 46 µW 3.4 µW
PGR 65 kHz 1.94 MHz 3.29 MHz 855 kHz 1.2 kHz 16 kHz 1.1 MHz 4.8 kHz 230KHz
assertions.certainty_reason: A table of figures the authors collected from their own and other works; not re-measured here.
assertions.reader_inference: The 3.29 MHz pair rate at 5.6 µW in the table does not appear in the body text. The body gives the pair rate only at the CAR peak (1.94 MHz at about -30.5 dBm, which is 0.9 µW).

assertions.value: The authors state that, because the photon pairs come from a non-resonant waveguide without microring enhancement, there is more freedom of wavelength selection and the instabilities of resonance shifting due to the thermo-optic effect or nonlinear phase modulation from a strong pump are avoided.
quotes: the photon pairs can be produced efficiently through our non-resonant waveguide without the nonlinearity enhancement by microring.
This allows more freedom of wavelength selection and avoid the instabilities of resonance shifting due to the thermo-optic effect
assertions.certainty_reason: An author argument; no stability measurement is reported in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no long-term stability test. Its comparison with resonant sources in Table 1 shows those sources reach higher CAR.

assertions.value: The authors state that, with a CAR higher than 1000 and a PGR of 1.94 MHz, their device can massively produce high quality photon pairs, and they present the a-Si:H/Si3N4 platform as an excellent and stable platform for photon-pair and single-photon generation.
quotes: With the CAR higher than 1000, our work features a high PGR of 1.94 MHz.
This shows that our device can massively produce high quality photon pairs.
assertions.certainty_reason: A characterization by the authors; no figure of merit for 'massively' is defined.
assertions.reader_inference: The CAR above 1000 and the PGR of 1.94 MHz are reported at the same pump power (about -30.5 dBm); the paper does not state a CAR above 1000 at higher pair rates.

assertions.value: The authors state that the CAR over the measured detuning range showcases a wide bandwidth for photon-pair generation that can be dispersion engineered into these devices.
quotes: This showcases a wide bandwidth for photon-pair generation that can be dispersion engineered into these devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement about what can be done; no dispersion-engineered device is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that the gH(2)(τ) measurement indicates their heterogeneous chip is a versatile single and paired photon source for a variety of quantum optical information technologies, and that gH(2)(τ) is important for ensuring the purity of a photon pair source.
quotes: This gH(2)(τ ) measurement indicates our heterogeneous chip is a versatile single and paired photon sources for a variety of quantum optical information technologies.
are important for ensuring the purity of photon pair source.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author interpretation; no application is demonstrated.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper demonstrates no downstream quantum information task, no indistinguishability measurement and no entanglement measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that correlated photon-pair sources are of great interest for quantum computing, teleportation, information processing, sensing and cryptography, and that a source with a broad and switchable bandwidth is essential for quantum frequency multiplexing and quantum memory, citing prior work.
quotes: correlated photon-pair sources are of great interest due to their applications in quantum computing, quantum teleportation, quantum information processing, quantum sensing, quantum cryptography
A photon pair source with a broad and switchable bandwidth is essential for applications such as quantum frequency multiplexing and quantum memory
assertions.certainty_reason: Background statements attributed to the cited literature.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Hemsley et al., that a-Si:H can be deposited at a lower temperature than crystalline silicon and thus incorporated in massive chip manufacturing processes.
quotes: a-Si:H can be easily deposited at a lower temperature and thus incorporated in massive chip manufacturing processes
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the increased coupling efficiency and low propagation losses of the SiNx waveguide allow a higher photon detection rate at much lower on-chip pump power, which enables a high CAR and a high photon pair generation rate.
quotes: with the increased coupling efficiency and low propagation losses of the SiNx waveguide, higher photon detection rate can be observed with much lower on-chip pump power.
This enables us to achieve a high CAR and high photon pair generation rate.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion; no single-layer control device is measured in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The only comparison is with the earlier a-Si:H result from Table 1, which differs in pump, filters and detectors.

assertions.value: The authors state that the multi-material deposition and low-loss interlayer couplers offer a way to integrate components from other materials in future photonic integrated circuits, naming chi(2) nonlinearity and electro-optic modulation from lithium niobate, laser sources from III-V materials, and photodetectors from germanium.
quotes: The multi-material deposition and low-loss interlayer couplers has enabled a way to combine different materials’ features onto the single platform
for example χ2 nonlinearity and electro-optic modulation from lithium niobate, laser source from III-V materials, and photodetectors from germanium
assertions.certainty_reason: A forward-looking statement; none of these integrations is demonstrated in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The photon-pair source, pump laser, filters and SNSPDs of this work are all off-chip; only the pair generation and routing are on-chip.
